claims.claim: Jainism is one of the three most ancient Indian religious traditions still in existence, alongside Hinduism and Buddhism, and scholars treat it as an independent tradition rather than a Hindu sect or a Buddhist heresy.

Scholars of religion generally hold that Jainism originated in the 7th-5th century BCE in the Ganges basin of eastern India; Jains hold that their tradition has no historical founder, and the first Jain figure for whom there is reasonable historical evidence is Parshvanatha, traditionally the 23rd tirthankara.

Mahavira (born Vardhamana) is traditionally the 24th and last tirthankara of the current age; tradition dates him to 599-527 BCE, while scholars treat him as a close contemporary of the Buddha and some prefer a later date around 540 BCE or after.

Ahimsa, nonviolence or non-injury toward all living creatures, is the most central Jain teaching and the heart of Jain ethics; Jains hold that animals, plants, and human beings all contain living souls of equal value that should be treated with respect and compassion.
The three jewels of Jain ethics are right faith (samyak darshana), right knowledge (samyak jnana), and right conduct (samyak charitra), understood as the path to liberation of the soul.

In Jain teaching karma is a subtle physical substance that fills the universe and is attracted to the soul through actions, words, and thoughts; liberation means getting rid of all karma attached to the soul, and karma operates without the intervention of any divine being.

Jains do not believe that the universe was created by a god; the universe is regarded as eternal and uncreated, and the perfected beings Jains venerate (the jinas, including the tirthankaras) are models to aspire to, not creators, judges, or helpers.

The five great vows (mahavratas) are nonviolence, truthfulness, not stealing, chastity (sexual restraint, with celibacy as the ideal), and non-attachment to possessions; monks and nuns follow them fully, while lay Jains follow the same principles in the less strict anuvratas (limited vows).

Fasting is very common in Jain spirituality, practiced at festivals and holy days and as penance, recalling Mahavira's asceticism; vegetarianism is the biggest practical expression of ahimsa in lay life, and lay Jains are expected to be vegetarian and to avoid occupations that cause harm.

Jains are divided into two major orders, the Digambara ('sky-clad') and the Svetambara ('white-clad'), which agree on the basics of the tradition but differ on monastic dress, the spiritual status of women, and which texts count as scripture.

The Agamas, the texts containing the teachings of Mahavira compiled by his disciples and long transmitted orally, are the canonical scriptures of Svetambara Jainism; the Digambara order holds that the original scriptures were lost and disagrees about the canon.

Today most of the more than six million Jains live in India, with diaspora communities in English-speaking countries, including about 25,000 in Britain (2006 estimate) and American communities established from the late 1960s; Jain ideas of ahimsa have influenced modern nonviolence movements, and Mahatma Gandhi was a famous advocate of ahimsa whose satyagraha ('truth-force') policy drew on it.

positions: Traditional dating: 599-527 BCE (Svetambara texts give 527 BCE for his death)

Scholarly framing: Britannica treats him as a close contemporary of the Buddha (traditionally 563-483 BCE, probably flourishing about a century later); BBC Religions notes some modern scholars prefer 540 BCE or even later
SEP records the traditional dates as 599-527/510 BCE
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents both framings: tradition dates Mahavira to 599-527 BCE, and scholars regard him as a close contemporary of the Buddha, with some preferring later dates.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the original Jain scriptures survived
positions: Svetambara view: the majority of the Agamas survived a famine around 350 BCE and were codified at Valabhi (453 or 456 CE)
Digambara view: all the Agamas were lost in the famine; the tradition has a different canonical history
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Described as a sectarian difference between the two orders; the lesson does not adjudicate which view is correct.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether a soul can attain liberation from a female body
positions: Digambara position: women cannot attain liberation without first being reborn as a man
Svetambara position: women can attain liberation
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented as one of the general differences between the two orders, named without adjudication.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether 'atheistic' is an accurate label for Jainism
positions: Some observers describe Jainism as atheistic because it affirms no creator god
Others, following the scholar Heinrich Zimmer, propose 'transtheistic,' because Jains venerate perfected beings (jinas) who are the ideal of every soul
The BBC notes the jinas are the beings 'most like gods' in Jain belief but they do not create, intervene, reward, or judge
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson describes the no-creator framing and notes that scholars debate the label rather than adopting a single one.

The no-creator framing is presented descriptively ('the tradition does not teach that the universe was created by a god'), not as an assertion that the tradition is atheistic in any absolute sense.
